title: Ripple Wins Final US Bank Charter: CEO Calls It ‘Big News’ Ahead of Swell
summary: Ripple has secured final federal approval for its national trust bank, advancing its plans for RLUSD reserve management and enterprise crypto custody. The charter places the institution under U.S. banking supervision and authorizes it to commence business. Final Charter Clears Path for Enterprise Cu...
content:
Ripple has secured final federal approval for its national trust bank, advancing its plans for RLUSD reserve management and enterprise crypto custody. The charter places the institution under U.S. banking supervision and authorizes it to commence business.

Key Takeaways

  • The bank will administer reserves for the benefit of RLUSD holders.
  • Standard Custody remains the stablecoin’s New York-regulated issuer.
  • RLUSD already supports Ripple’s payments and prime brokerage operations.

Final Charter Clears Path for Enterprise Custody

Enterprises will gain a federally supervised platform for stablecoin infrastructure and digital asset custody when Ripple National Trust Bank (RNTB) opens. Blockchain infrastructure provider Ripple disclosed the final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) on Oct. 26.

Brad Garlinghouse, CEO of Ripple, called the decision “Big news” ahead of Swell, Ripple’s annual blockchain and finance conference. His comments on federal supervision appeared on X that day. “This gives Ripple a federally supervised platform to support $RLUSD and provide digital asset custody to enterprises. We’ve always said crypto and banks work better together — this is what that looks like,” Garlinghouse said, adding:

“Real innovation, real accountability, federal oversight. The revolution isn’t happening outside the system. It’s happening from within it.”

Conditional authorization preceded the final decision, with Ripple receiving its conditional national trust bank approval on Dec. 12, 2025. The latest authorization completes RNTB’s organization process and establishes its approved business activities.

RLUSD Issuance Continues Under New York Oversight

Standard Custody & Trust Company (SCTC), Ripple’s limited purpose trust company regulated by the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), will continue issuing RLUSD. The token is a stablecoin designed to track the U.S. dollar. RNTB adds federal supervision to the infrastructure backing it.

Federal regulators originally included Ripple in a broader round of five conditional trust bank charter approvals. That group also encompassed First National Digital Currency Bank and proposed conversions of state trust companies operated by Bitgo, Fidelity Digital Assets, and Paxos.

Reserve assets include U.S. dollar deposits, U.S. government securities, and other cash equivalents, with BNY as the primary reserve custodian. Ripple publishes monthly independent third-party attestations covering circulating supply and backing assets. Launched in December 2024, RLUSD operates across Ripple’s payments infrastructure and serves as collateral within Ripple Prime, its prime brokerage business.

Institutional Uses Extend Across Payments and Trading

Eligible institutions also gained Standard Chartered custody for RLUSD on the XRP Ledger earlier this month. Its Dubai International Financial Centre branch operates in a financial hub with its own legal framework. A separate planned integration with Ripple and LMAX Group, an operator of foreign exchange and digital asset trading venues, would enable trading collateral use, subject to testing, documentation, and applicable approvals.

Jack McDonald, Ripple’s senior vice president of stablecoins, outlined RNTB’s reserve and custody functions on X on Oct. 26:

“This is much more than a charter on paper. RNTB is designed to manage reserves supporting $RLUSD, serve as collateral trustee for RLUSD holders, and provide regulated digital asset custody — bringing federal banking supervision directly into the infrastructure institutions use.”

Ripple will continue working with the OCC, NYDFS, and other regulators as RNTB begins operations and the United States implements the GENIUS Act, a law establishing a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins.

TL;DR: Visa, BILL and Billtrust are piloting trusted AI agents that complete approved invoice payments through supplier portals.

The next stage of automated payments may depend less on how fast a transfer settles and more on proving who authorised it. Visa, BILL and Billtrust announced an October 20 live pilot allowing trusted AI agents to initiate and complete approved buyer-invoice payments through supplier portals.

The project uses Visa’s Intelligent Commerce tools, including Trusted Agent Protocol, to authenticate software agents to portals that historically expected a human user. The companies emphasise preserving supplier oversight and controls. This is a limited business-payments pilot, not an announcement that autonomous systems now have open-ended authority to spend on behalf of anyone.

For cryptocurrency wallets, there is a close parallel. An agent could technically sign and broadcast transfers today, but the difficult questions concern budgets, permissions, revocation, audit trails and responsibility when the agent makes an error. Those are exactly the issues businesses will have to solve before automatic onchain commerce becomes routine.

Visa’s experiment is not itself a public-blockchain settlement launch. Its relevance to crypto is the permission layer: whichever rail eventually carries an automated payment, businesses will want evidence that the software initiating it was known, constrained and acting within instructions. That security problem is becoming a commercial product category of its own.

title: Keystone breach deepens: Hackers stole key used to verify wallets as genuine
summary: Keystone initially disclosed a leak of customer information but has since disclosed that hackers also stole a key that could allow counterfeit wallets to pass authenticity checks.
content:
Hardware wallet maker Keystone said an attacker who breached its website last week also stole a key used to verify the authenticity of its devices, widening the scope of an incident initially disclosed as a customer data leak.

In a statement Monday, Keystone said the stolen authentication key could allow attackers to produce counterfeit wallets that pass its authenticity checks.

“These devices could then be sold or shipped to customers, who might unknowingly use them as genuine products, potentially resulting in asset theft,” Keystone said.  

The incident adds to a series of attacks targeting hardware wallet manufacturers this year. 

Earlier this month, Ledger asked resellers across Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to suspend sales following reports that devices sold in the region contained unauthorized implants capable of capturing recovery phrases.

In late July, Coldcard manufacturer Coinkite issued a warning to users after attackers exploited a bug that caused its devices to generate wallet seeds with less entropy than intended, resulting in the theft of millions of dollars in crypto.

Keystone to destroy more than 18,000 devices with old key

In its latest update, Keystone said the attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party monitoring tool used by its website to escalate privileges. 

“This enabled the attacker to obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices.” 

Keystone said it plans to destroy 18,835 devices in its inventory that contain the compromised key and has suspended production shipments of all devices using it.

 The company said shipments would resume once it begins producing devices with a new authentication key.

Keystone said devices manufactured and delivered before the Oct. 20 incident should be considered safe and that their authenticity checks remain trustworthy.

However, it could not guarantee the authenticity of devices delivered after that date and urged affected customers to contact its support team for additional verification.

Keystone confirms 25,964 buyer records leaked

Keystone also disclosed the extent of the customer data breach, saying its website’s Shopify store had generated 51,083 buyer records.

Of those, 25,119 had been deleted per its 180-day data retention policy. 

However, the remaining 25,964 records dating from 2024 to 2026 were stolen by the attacker. Keystone said the older entries were not deleted due to a failure in its automated tool used to handle bulk erasure of data. 

“The tool did not operate reliably. Some erasure tasks failed, and we did not detect and address these failures in time, resulting in certain personal information being retained beyond the permitted period,” Keystone said. 

Related: Keystone says website breach exposed hardware wallet buyers’ addresses

In addition, the attacker managed to steal another 12,873 customer checkout records retained by Shopify — information from purchases that had not been completed. 

Keystone said it had contacted Shopify to request the deletion of personal information in checkout records retained for more than 30 days.

The incident echoes a June 2020 data breach at Ledger that exposed more than 1 million email addresses, along with customer names, phone numbers and physical addresses. The leaked information fueled years of phishing attempts targeting affected users.

Other hardware wallet manufacturers have also suffered breaches involving customer information and third-party services this year.

In August, Trezor disclosed a breach at its shipping partner that exposed customer information, with the number of affected users expanding to more than 80,000 in September. 

SafePal also reported an order-tracking vulnerability in August that exposed data belonging to nearly 40,000 customers, while BitBox was targeted in a September phishing campaign involving a compromised third-party email provider.

title: Aviva Invests $66 Million in Tokenized Sterling Fund on XRP Ledger
summary: Aviva has invested $66 million in a tokenized share class of its Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger. The launch extends its partnership with Ripple and expands blockchain access to conventional money market investments. Aviva Commits $66 Million to Tokenized Sterling Shares Eligible investors...
content:
Aviva has invested $66 million in a tokenized share class of its Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger. The launch extends its partnership with Ripple and expands blockchain access to conventional money market investments.

Key Takeaways

  • The underlying Sterling Liquidity Fund holds approximately GBP 22 billion.
  • Investments across Aviva Investors’ two tokenized share classes exceed $116 million.
  • Eligible investors retain the conventional fund’s protections and liquidity.

Aviva Commits $66 Million to Tokenized Sterling Shares

Eligible investors can now access Aviva Investors’ largest fund through tokenized shares issued and managed on the XRP Ledger. Aviva’s asset management business and blockchain infrastructure provider Ripple announced the launch on Oct. 26. Aviva’s GBP 50 million investment, equivalent to $66 million, went into the new share class of the Sterling Liquidity Fund, which oversees approximately GBP 22 billion overall.

Combined investment across the firm’s two tokenized share classes now exceeds GBP 86 million, or $116 million, according to the announcement. Those holdings span the sterling offering and its dollar-denominated counterpart. Aviva Investors CEO Mark Versey said:

“This expansion of our tokenised offering shows our clear intent to be a leader in this area and sets the groundwork for a future expansion of our capabilities.”

July’s launch introduced the tokenized U.S. dollar liquidity fund share class, establishing the firm’s first blockchain-based offering. The sterling version brings its lineup to two currencies.

Digital Twin Model Preserves Fund Protections

Holdings in the new share class use a digital twin model that creates a blockchain copy of an existing investment while preserving the existing off-chain fund structure. This approach applies real-world asset tokenization to conventional fund interests. Investors retain the same investment objective, risk profile, liquidity characteristics, and regulatory protections as the original fund, which launched in 2002.

Under UCITS, the European Union’s Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities framework, the Ireland-domiciled fund follows common investment and investor-protection rules. It targets low-risk returns and daily liquidity through high-grade, sterling-denominated short-term debt instruments.

Custody and tokenization support come from institutional digital asset custodian Komainu, which safeguards digital holdings, alongside infrastructure platform Licuido, which helps asset managers tokenize and trade financial assets. Eligible investors need digital wallets to access the share class. The underlying fund assets remain with The Bank of New York Mellon, the fund’s custodian.

Aviva Deal Was Ripple’s First With a European Investment Manager

February’s agreement established the fund tokenization partnership, with plans to bring traditional fund structures to the XRP Ledger during 2026 and beyond. Ripple supplies blockchain infrastructure for issuing and managing the tokenized investments.

That agreement marked Ripple’s first European investment manager partnership and Aviva Investors’ initial move toward incorporating tokenized products into its existing offering.

Brazil’s CSD BR, an operator that registers securities, maintains ownership records, and settles transactions, is also working with Ripple on blockchain copies of fund ownership records. This process, called ownership mirroring, starts with investment fund shares from Brazilian investment bank BTG Pactual. The blockchain copies supplement CSD BR’s systems, which remain the official ownership record.

title: Spacex Secures $40B as Musk Predicts Most Neoclouds Will Fail
summary: Spacex has secured a roughly $40 billion equipment financing commitment as CEO Elon Musk predicts failures among specialized AI cloud providers. The conditional agreement would fund computing hardware, with deliveries expected in the first half of 2027. Spacex Secures Conditional Financing for AI Eq...
content:
Spacex has secured a roughly $40 billion equipment financing commitment as CEO Elon Musk predicts failures among specialized AI cloud providers. The conditional agreement would fund computing hardware, with deliveries expected in the first half of 2027.

Key Takeaways

  • The equipment lease is expected to close before year-end, subject to conditions.
  • An Apollo-managed entity would purchase the hardware and lease it to Spacex.
  • Musk predicts widespread failures and consolidation among specialized providers.

Spacex Secures Conditional Financing for AI Equipment

Apollo Global Management disclosed the approximately $40 billion equipment financing commitment on Oct. 26, following Spacex CEO Elon Musk’s comments on X a day earlier. The rocket, satellite internet, and AI company entered a binding commitment for an equipment lease, with closing expected before year-end, subject to specified conditions.

Under the GPU equipment financing commitment, an entity managed by investment manager Apollo Global Management would purchase graphics processing units, or GPUs, and related hardware for Spacex to lease. The master finance lease would establish terms for separate equipment batches, with approximately $40 billion in expected aggregate principal payments.

Apollo’s announcement states:

“It represents the largest committed GPU financing, underscoring the strength of Spacex’s infrastructure capabilities.”

In an X post about Spacex’s investment-grade credit standing, Musk attributed the company’s ability to borrow to its credit rating, which indicates relatively low default risk:

“Spacex closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.”

His follow-up GPU financing explanation described the arrangement as primarily callable debt, generally permitting repayment before maturity under specified terms. He expected chip deliveries in the first and second quarters of 2027 and little effect this quarter. The subsequent disclosure identifies a lease commitment whose closing remains pending.

Musk Warns Specialized Cloud Providers Face Failures

Specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, rent computing infrastructure designed for artificial intelligence workloads. Musk argued that debt markets had largely restricted funding for businesses without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. His forecast followed investor Chamath Palihapitiya’s concerns about construction delays and unused computing capacity in 2027.

Musk predicted:

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.”

Borrowers must generate enough cash to meet debt repayment obligations alongside operating costs, while lenders assess their ability to pay. Those creditors’ repayment claims differ from shareholders’ ownership interests. Musk presented Spacex’s established businesses as an advantage in obtaining capital, rather than treating AI demand alone as sufficient support.

Elsewhere in the industry, Stack Infrastructure was reportedly seeking a $6 billion Melbourne data center loan earlier this month. That proposed borrowing remained a fundraising effort, providing a separate example of developers seeking substantial capital for computing facilities.

Computing Plans Drive Spending and Manufacturing Targets

Capital expenditures reached $19.6 billion in the third quarter, Spacex’s quarterly earnings presentation disclosed Oct. 20. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen projected fourth-quarter spending of $35 billion to $40 billion as the company adds computing capacity.

Software development also expanded through the company’s $60 billion Cursor acquisition in August. Cursor is an AI-powered coding platform that helps developers write and modify software. Its earlier partnership with Spacex provided computing infrastructure for model training, the process of teaching AI systems to recognize patterns using data.

Longer-term plans include the Terafab semiconductor manufacturing project being developed with Tesla. Musk outlined a May or June 2027 target for a functional test chip at a research facility in Austin. He described production in the third or fourth quarter of 2028 at Gibbons Creek, the planned main site in Grimes County, Texas, as an aggressive goal.

title: Ault Blockchain – Silver First, Then Everything Else
summary: Milton “Todd” Ault III is the founder of Ault Blockchain and executive chairman of Hyperscale Data (NYSE American: GPUS). Hyperscale Data is an AI data center company whose subsidiaries are building two things: Ault Blockchain, a finance-first, EVM-compatible layer one, and Ault Markets, the trading...
content:
Skip to content

Milton “Todd” Ault III is the founder of Ault Blockchain and executive chairman of Hyperscale Data (NYSE American: GPUS). Hyperscale Data is an AI data center company whose subsidiaries are building two things: Ault Blockchain, a finance-first, EVM-compatible layer one, and Ault Markets, the trading venue that sits on top of it. Ault has spent 37 years in traditional finance, starting at Dean Witter and running a hedge fund for much of that time. He has been involved with Bitcoin since 2011, later spent hundreds of millions of dollars building a mining operation, and says he was debanked around ten times before the US regulatory climate changed.

The link will open a new window. Click the menu and down arrow to download the file.

Why you should listen

Most new layer ones are built to trade perpetual futures. Ault thinks the bigger gap is in spot commodities. Trillions of dollars of metals trade every year, yet only about $5 billion has been tokenized, and buying physical silver still usually means a trip to a local dealer. Ault Markets opened to invited users in early October, and the group has since tokenized its first 5,000 troy ounces of silver, vaulted at The Wyoming Reserve. Ault describes the end goal: trade silver, gold, platinum, and palladium around the clock without KYC, complete KYC only when you want physical delivery, and have the metal shipped within one to three days. Behind the metals he plans tokenized convertible loans and structured notes, and he wants roughly 400 real-world assets on chain within two years. New offices in Dubai and Singapore are part of that push.

The company sold Bitcoin to help fund its Michigan campus, which has switched off its miners and moved to AI hosting under a contract the company values at up to $1.2 billion. Ault does not expect miners to switch back. He compares AI to the early internet, with one difference: the internet had an adoption problem, while AI has a capacity problem. He still calls himself something of a Bitcoin maximalist. He describes Bitcoin as the pristine collateral at the base of future finance and gives credit to Michael Saylor for reading the history of money correctly.

The hot take round adds more. Ault calls himself multi-chain and predicts that reserve banking as we know it is finished. He expects more than $10 trillion in tokenized assets within a decade, and he wants the US to hold Bitcoin as a strategic reserve and issue Bitcoin-backed debt. For a sign that the future is already here, he points to onchain perps: when he asks rooms of Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley advisors whether they have used Hyperliquid, almost nobody raises a hand. On sci-fi, he names Battlestar Galactica and Star Wars before settling on The Matrix. Then, live on air, he asks his AI assistant Jenna to look up Andy, and she does.

TL;DR: Visa says Inyo Global is the first enabler to bring its stablecoin-enabled Visa Direct prefunding into production for eligible clients.

Stablecoins are often discussed as an alternative to established payment networks. Visa’s latest move shows how they can instead become a funding component inside one. On October 15, the company said its Visa Direct stablecoin-enabled prefunding had moved into production through Inyo Global, its first enabling processor.

The mechanism addresses how payment providers position money for international transfers. Rather than waiting for traditional bank rails to move funds during restricted operating windows, eligible clients can use stablecoin capability to support funding through Visa Direct. The announcement describes an initial commercial deployment, not blanket access for every cardholder or every territory.

For crypto markets, the development is less about a speculative token narrative than evidence of infrastructure buying interest. Payment businesses care whether a transfer can be funded at the required time and reconciled reliably afterward. Stablecoins offer a potential improvement in availability, while traditional systems still provide compliance, distribution and local payout connections.

There is no reason to assume lower consumer fees or universal instant settlement without a fuller breakdown of corridors and pricing. But the production milestone matters because it asks stablecoin rails to solve an existing business problem under live operating constraints, rather than merely demonstrate a transaction in a controlled pilot.

title: Ripple Takes RLUSD Into Corporate Cash Management With 24/7 Returns
summary: Ripple Treasury is targeting idle corporate cash with returns on qualifying holdings of Ripple USD (RLUSD), its dollar-backed stablecoin. The expansion pairs operations outside banking hours with artificial intelligence tools for managing cash and payments. RLUSD Returns Target Idle Operating Cash E...
content:
Ripple Treasury is targeting idle corporate cash with returns on qualifying holdings of Ripple USD (RLUSD), its dollar-backed stablecoin. The expansion pairs operations outside banking hours with artificial intelligence tools for managing cash and payments.

Key Takeaways

  • Returns target operating cash left idle overnight, over weekends, and during holidays.
  • Qualifying digital assets must be held in a Ripple wallet and meet program rules.
  • AI tools coordinate forecasting, reconciliation, liquidity management, and payments.

RLUSD Returns Target Idle Operating Cash

Eligible businesses can earn returns on operating cash outside traditional banking hours through Ripple’s 24/7 Returns offering, unveiled at Swell on Oct. 26. The program covers qualifying digital assets held in a Ripple wallet, including RLUSD, and requires participants to meet eligibility rules. Businesses do not need to manage the underlying digital asset transactions themselves.

RLUSD, Ripple’s U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin, is designed to maintain a value of $1 per token. Stablecoins support blockchain payments and settlement while targeting a stable value. Their reliability depends on reserves and redemption arrangements, which determine how holders exchange tokens for the underlying currency.

“As AI accelerates decision-making and digital rails enable money to move around the clock, businesses need systems that can keep pace,” Renaat Ver Eecke, senior vice president of Ripple Treasury, said, adding:

“Our vision is to bring treasury management, intelligence, and execution together, giving finance teams the ability to act faster and operate continuously without adding complexity or sacrificing control.”

AI Links Forecasting With Payments

Ripple Treasury uses software to coordinate financial tasks with help from its GSmart artificial intelligence tools. Functions include determining available cash, forecasting future balances, matching financial records, managing liquidity, and processing payments. Ripple describes the integration as connecting decisions with execution while reducing manual work.

As of March, 46% of organizations represented in the Association for Financial Professionals’ (AFP) Liquidity Survey reported holding more U.S. cash than a year earlier. Ripple also cited the survey’s finding that 86% of treasury professionals would choose real-time money market funds if they met their organizations’ investment policies.

American Airlines, Trax, Christian Louboutin, Subway, Adecco, and Kingfisher are among the businesses named in Ripple’s treasury announcement. The company describes a strategy combining treasury management, payments, liquidity, stablecoins, and custody to simplify operations across conventional and digital payment systems.

Bank Custody Expands RLUSD’s Institutional Reach

The platform’s origins trace to Ripple’s $1 billion GTreasury acquisition announcement in October 2025, marking its entry into enterprise treasury management. GTreasury provides software for managing corporate cash and financial operations, bringing forecasting and risk management capabilities to Ripple’s digital asset infrastructure.

Institutional infrastructure expanded when Standard Chartered began offering RLUSD custody on Oct. 12 for tokens issued on the XRP Ledger, through its Dubai International Financial Centre branch. The bank also joined Ripple and LMAX Group, an institutional trading infrastructure operator, on an arrangement to make RLUSD eligible collateral for agreed LMAX products while the tokens remain in custody.

Regulatory requirements also shape stablecoin operations, with Ripple outlining differences in reserve rules and supervision in September. The company distinguished money transmitter licenses, state trust charters, and banking oversight, which impose different capital requirements and protections if an issuer fails. State trust charters authorize trust companies to operate under state supervision.

title: Bitcoin Bottom May Be Near as 30,000 Wallets Disappear: Santiment
summary: Bitcoin may be approaching a local bottom as smaller holders retreat, according to Santiment’s latest analysis. Falling wallet participation could support a recovery, with $80,000 support and a move back above $82,500 central to the setup. Wallet Declines Signal a Possible Bitcoin Bottom A potential...
content:
Bitcoin may be approaching a local bottom as smaller holders retreat, according to Santiment’s latest analysis. Falling wallet participation could support a recovery, with $80,000 support and a move back above $82,500 central to the setup.

Key Takeaways

  • Nonempty bitcoin wallets fell roughly 30K to about 59.95 million.
  • Continued wallet declines alongside price strength would reinforce the signal.
  • A sustained break below $79K would delay the potential bottom.

Wallet Declines Signal a Possible Bitcoin Bottom

A potential bitcoin bottom may be taking shape as smaller holders appear to abandon positions after weeks of stagnant prices. Blockchain analytics platform Santiment shared that assessment on Oct. 26. Its analysis of declining wallet participation identifies roughly 30K fewer nonempty wallets since Oct. 16, bringing the total near 59.95 million.

The firm’s interpretation centers on retail capitulation, a term describing smaller investors giving up and selling during market weakness. A contrarian signal suggests prices may move against the crowd’s expectations, with widespread pessimism potentially indicating that a recovery is approaching. Santiment views these departures as historically more constructive for prices than buyers chasing rallies.

Retail Behavior Offers a Historical Comparison

An earlier contraction in smaller-holder groups preceded bitcoin’s recovery above $85K, providing a comparison for Santiment’s latest interpretation. Its September assessment identified 69,494 addresses leaving two balance groups during July and August. Those groups held between 0.1 and 1 BTC and between 1 and 10 BTC, respectively. Departures could reflect selling, consolidation, or movements outside those ranges.

Address balances change when coins move, so the number of funded addresses differs from the number of individual investors. Transaction inputs and outputs reassign coins, with change often returning to another address controlled by the sender. One investor can control multiple addresses, and an emptied address can receive funds again.

By early October, the firm’s analysis described an obstacle: small holders were continuing to accumulate despite falling prices. Santiment’s Oct. 9 assessment found wallets holding 10 to 10K BTC had added more than 85K BTC over roughly three weeks. Meanwhile, wallets holding less than 0.01 BTC had continued increasing, which the firm viewed as an impediment to a stronger recovery.

$80,000 Support and $82,500 Recovery Test

Recent price weakness adds another challenge to the recovery scenario, with bitcoin losing a level that had supported earlier trading. By Oct. 24, BTC had fallen below its 50-day moving average, a measure of average daily closing prices over that period. The breach followed roughly two months in which the indicator had acted as support.

Separately, demand and investor profitability showed weaknesses in an Oct. 21 assessment by Cryptoquant contributor Darkfost. The analyst highlighted a Bull Score Index decline from 80 to 60. The index combines 10 measures, including demand, network activity, liquidity, and profitability, to evaluate the market environment.

Santiment stated:

“$80K is the immediate battleground. If wallets keep declining while BTC holds $80K and reclaims roughly $82.5K, the contrarian bottom signal becomes much stronger. A sustained break below the recent $79K area would delay that setup and suggest capitulation still has further to run.”

title: Ripple wins final US approval for national trust bank
summary: The approval clears the way for Ripple to manage reserves backing its RLUSD stablecoin and provide digital asset custody.
content:
The approval clears the way for Ripple to manage reserves backing its RLUSD stablecoin and provide digital asset custody.

Ripple announced Monday that its national trust bank has secured final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

The approval completes the chartering process for Ripple National Trust Bank (RNTB), which received conditional approval from the OCC in December 2025.

The federally supervised trust bank is authorized to manage reserves backing Ripple USD (RLUSD), act as collateral trustee for the benefit of RLUSD holders and provide digital asset custody services, according to Ripple.

RLUSD will continue to be issued by Standard Custody & Trust Company, Ripple’s limited purpose trust company regulated by the New York Department of Financial Services.

“We’ve always said crypto and banks work better together — this is what that looks like. Real innovation, real accountability, federal oversight,” Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse said on X on Monday.

Ripple follows Circle, which secured final OCC approval in July. Other crypto firms remain at the conditional approval stage, including Coinbase, which received its preliminary green light in April, and Crypto.com and Stripe-owned Bridge, which received conditional approvals in February.

A national trust bank is a federally chartered institution focused on holding and managing assets on behalf of clients. Unlike a typical commercial bank, most national trust banks do not accept deposits or make loans and do not carry Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insurance, according to the OCC.

Bitcoin developers have gathered all around the world in places like Austin, Berlin, and Florianópolis, to name a few. In early 2028, a group of them plans to meet at the bottom of the world. bitcoin++ has announced Antarctica: Cold Storage Edition, scheduled for January 24 to February 5, 2028. There are only 22 spots available.

The event pairs a technical conference with an expedition ship that departs from Ushuaia, Argentina, crosses the Drake Passage, explores the Antarctic Peninsula, and returns to Ushuaia.

The event plays on bitcoin’s cold storage, the practice of keeping keys offline. The organizers describe the trip as a way to take the conversation somewhere colder, with room for discussions that would otherwise fit into a hallway.

bitcoin++ runs technical conferences, workshops, and hackathons for bitcoin developers. The series began in Austin in 2022 and has since held events in Berlin, Florianópolis, Buenos Aires, Mexico City, Riga, Istanbul, Taipei, Las Vegas, Vienna, Nairobi, Toronto, and Seoul. Each edition carries a theme, from “learn me a bitcoin” in Austin in 2022 to “lightning” in Berlin in 2025. 

The organization counts some 20 archived editions. Its next conference, bitcoin++ Seoul, privacy edition, takes place November 5 and 6, 2026.

Penguins, parkas, and private keys

The trip runs 13 days and 12 nights. The ship leaves Ushuaia on January 24 and crosses the Drake Passage to the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula. Possible stops include Neko Harbour, Paradise Bay, Port Lockroy, and the Lemaire Channel. 

According to the trip’s website, activities may include kayaking, camping, hiking, snowshoeing, and Zodiac outings. The organizers note that weather, ice, and expedition decisions determine where the ship lands.

The conference follows an unconference format. Attendees propose the talks, demos, and discussions. The ship will have Starlink and a private room for impromptu hackathons and working sessions.

Cost and booking

Reservations are open right now. Fares are quoted in US dollars per person and range from $14,900 in a four-person cabin to $16,700 in a two-person cabin. Passengers may pay in five equal installments or pay in full at signup. Paying the full fare in bitcoin reduces the cost by 5%. The cost of the fare includes parkas.

The final payment is due October 1, 2027. Medical, evacuation, and repatriation insurance is required and purchased separately. Sponsors can place their brands on the expedition parkas. Placements range from $5,000 to $25,000, and each covers about 22 parkas.

The expedition explores the Antarctic Peninsula, not the geographic South Pole.

Micah Zimmerman

Micah first discovered Bitcoin in 2018 but remained a skeptic on the sidelines for too long. Since 2021, he has covered crypto and business and now works as a news reporter for Bitcoin Magazine, based in North Carolina.

Investors can trade US stocks through digital apps at almost any hour, but moving the cash needed to fund those trades still runs into banking cutoffs. A newly announced partnership between DriveWealth and Ripple aims to close that gap using stablecoin infrastructure.

DriveWealth supplies brokerage infrastructure to more than 100 partners. If the promised settlement improvements reach production, they could become visible inside familiar investing applications rather than as a standalone crypto product. The test will be whether stablecoin funding makes the end-to-end customer experience measurably better.

title: Monero Hashrate Nears Record Highs as XMR Price Gains 70% in a Year
summary: Monero’s network hashrate is hovering near historic highs, but its mining distribution tells an equally compelling story. On Monday, network computing power stood near 7.12 GH/s, with three major mining pools controlling approximately 60% of that total. Monero’s Mining Power Climbs as Three Pools Do...
content:
Monero’s network hashrate is hovering near historic highs, but its mining distribution tells an equally compelling story. On Monday, network computing power stood near 7.12 GH/s, with three major mining pools controlling approximately 60% of that total.

Key Takeaways

  • Monero’s network hashrate reached an estimated 7.12 GH/s on Oct. 26.
  • SupportXMR, Nanopool and Kryptex collectively accounted for approximately 60% of Monero’s computing power.
  • Monero’s RandomX mining model faces concentration concerns following Qubic’s 2025 offensive.

Monero’s Mining Power Climbs as Three Pools Dominate the Hashrate Race

Monero’s mining network is going great guns, with hashrate estimates approaching historic highs while a handful of mining pools command most of the computational firepower. On Oct. 26, 2026, mining distribution data showed around 7.12 gigahash per second (GH/s) securing the privacy-focused blockchain.

The figures paint an intriguing picture of a cryptocurrency deliberately engineered for accessible CPU mining, yet increasingly shaped by industrial-scale competition, concentrated pool participation, and specialized hardware.

Three Mining Pools Command Nearly 60% of Monero’s Hashpower

Mining distribution figures from Miningpoolstats show SupportXMR leading the pack with approximately 1.87 GH/s, followed by Nanopool at 1.23 GH/s and Kryptex at 1.17 GH/s. Together, those three pools represent approximately 4.27 GH/s, or 60% of the estimated network total. SupportXMR alone accounts for roughly 26.3%, while Nanopool and Kryptex represent approximately 17.3% and 16.4%, respectively.

Hashvault follows with 730.76 megahash per second (MH/s), while C3Pool contributes 481.17 MH/s. P2Pool’s largest listed segment supplies another 473 MH/s, offering miners a decentralized alternative to conventional pool operators. The figures don’t establish that three entities own 60% of Monero’s mining equipment. Pool operators coordinate computing power contributed by independent miners, who can redirect their machines elsewhere.

Nevertheless, the distribution shows how mining coordination can become concentrated even when participation remains technically accessible.

Monero Mining Pool Distribution, Oct. 26, 2026

P2Pool473.00 MH/s6.6%

Source: Miningpoolstats, Oct. 26, 2026, at 6 p.m. ET. Network hashrate estimated at 7.12 GH/s. Percentages are approximate, and P2Pool figures reflect its largest listed segment.

Qubic’s 2025 Mining Offensive Still Looms Large

Monero’s elevated hashrate follows a contentious 2025 campaign in which Qubic directed substantial outside computing resources toward the network. Qubic claimed it temporarily controlled more than 51% of Monero’s hashrate, equivalent to approximately 2.7 to 3 GH/s at the time. Short blockchain reorganizations and orphaned blocks accompanied the episode, although the network continued operating.

The confrontation rocked discussions about Monero’s security model, particularly whether CPU-friendly mining alone could prevent coordinated entities from amassing considerable computing power. While the network is humming along at 7.12 GH/s, it is still below the all-time high logged earlier this year. Coinwarz data shows that the Monero network reached 7.54 GH/s at block height 3589072.

RandomX Keeps CPUs Competitive, but Bitmain Enters the Picture

Monero relies on RandomX, a proof-of-work (PoW) algorithm introduced in November 2019 to favor general-purpose CPUs over conventional application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). RandomX combines random program execution, memory-intensive operations and complex calculations to discourage the extreme hardware specialization associated with bitcoin mining. Bitcoin’s pool distribution concentration is no better, as the top three mining pools command 59.51% at the time of writing.

As far as XMR, Bitmain has challenged the decentralized mining premise with dedicated RandomX equipment. Its Antminer X5, released in 2023, delivers approximately 212 kilohash per second (KH/s) while consuming 1,350 watts. The X5 unit was sold for $2,999. A Bitmain X9, which delivers 1 megahash per second (MH/s) of hashpower, was sold for $5,599, and gets an estimated $28.27 per day according to current XMR prices. This makes RandomX the second most profitable PoW mining algorithm today, just under Zcash’s Equihash. According to Bitmain’s shop, both the X5 and X9 units are sold out.

Monero’s Growing Security Budget Faces a Decentralization Test

The privacy coin Monero produces blocks approximately every two minutes, awarding miners a permanent base reward of 0.6 XMR plus transaction fees. That tail emission creates roughly 432 new XMR daily, providing continuing incentives for miners regardless of transaction activity. Higher network hashrate generally raises the computing resources required to challenge Monero’s consensus, but distribution matters as much as raw computational strength.

A great deal of that strength derived from XMR’s price jump this past year. Over the last 12 months, monero has climbed 70% against the U.S. dollar while year-to-date stats show a 37% gain. XMR’s price nearly doubling in value in a year has clearly attracted mining interest across a myriad of mining pools, not just the top three. Today, the latest figures show the five largest listed pools collectively directing roughly 77% of the estimated network hashrate.

That’s a substantial concentration of coordinated mining activity, even though the underlying hardware may belong to thousands of independent participants. For Monero, the pressing question isn’t whether its miners can produce more hashes. It’s whether the network can keep that expanding computing power sufficiently dispersed to resist the next coordinated challenge.

title: Binance Founder CZ Backs BNB Chain’s New High-Speed Layer 1 Network
summary: BNB Chain is preparing a new EVM-compatible Layer 1 that will run alongside the main network, using BNB for gas, staking, and governance rather than issuing a new token. BNB Chain Keeps BNB at Center of New Layer 1 Expansion The BNB Chain ecosystem is preparing a second Layer 1 built for speed, but ...
content:
BNB Chain is preparing a new EVM-compatible Layer 1 that will run alongside the main network, using BNB for gas, staking, and governance rather than issuing a new token.

Key Takeaways

  • BNB Chain is building a second EVM L1 with 200ms blocks, using BNB for gas, staking, and governance.
  • The new chain targets high-speed trading and payments, while BNB Chain keeps its existing DeFi ecosystem.
  • A public testnet is due by the end of 2026, with mainnet planned for early 2027.

BNB Chain Keeps BNB at Center of New Layer 1 Expansion

The BNB Chain ecosystem is preparing a second Layer 1 built for speed, but it is not abandoning its original network (currently called BNB Smart Chain) or creating another token.

Updated documentation published Oct. 22 outlines a new high-performance L1, currently unnamed, that will operate in parallel with BNB Smart Chain and connect to it through a native bridge.

BNB will remain the shared economic asset across both networks, covering gas, staking, and governance. Binance Founder Changpeng Zhao summed up the strategy on X: “Multiple chains, one coin.”

New Chain Targets Trading and Payments

The new Layer 1 is being designed around workloads where latency matters.

Target specifications include roughly 200-millisecond block times, about 20-millisecond transaction pre-confirmations, and sub-second transaction ordering. That makes the architecture particularly relevant for high-frequency crypto trading, onchain order books, and real-time payments.

The strategy reflects a broader shift in blockchain infrastructure. Networks are increasingly being optimized for specialized financial applications rather than forcing every workload onto one general-purpose chain.

BNB Smart Chain will continue supporting its existing DeFi and application ecosystem, while the new chain is intended to handle more demanding use cases.

BNB Remains the Economic Center

The decision not to launch a separate token is significant.

BNB will be used across both chains, meaning activity on the new network could theoretically increase demand for the same asset rather than fragmenting liquidity across two native tokens.

That structure also gives developers and users a more familiar transition path.

BNB was trading around $743 when details of the plan circulated, though the new architecture is still months away from public deployment and its eventual effect on token demand remains uncertain. The price of BNB peaked in Oct. 2025 at a price of about $1,370, which means it’s down about 46% in the last year.

For holders, the key question will be whether additional transaction activity translates into meaningful gas, staking, or governance usage.

Testnet Is Planned Before Year-End

Development is already underway. BNB Chain says an internal multi-validator devnet is operating now. A public testnet is planned for the end of 2026, with mainnet targeted for early 2027.

The timing comes as high-performance onchain trading venues such as Hyperliquid, Lighter, and Aster raise expectations around speed and execution quality.

That competitive pressure appears central to the new L1 thesis.

BNB Chain is no longer positioning itself only as a low-cost general-purpose network. It is building infrastructure aimed directly at the next generation of onchain finance.

The architecture may be new, but the economic bet is familiar: keep BNB at the center while giving demanding applications a faster place to run.

TL;DR: Ripple Prime says eligible institutional clients can trade perpetual swaps referencing more than 100 traditional markets through its new offering.

Exposure to traditional markets is increasingly being packaged for venues that never close. Ripple Prime said on October 15 that it had introduced support for real-world-asset perpetual swaps covering more than 100 reference markets, including equities, ETFs, commodities and currencies.

The contracts reference perpetual futures listed by Trade.xyz on Hyperliquid, while Ripple Prime acts as principal to institutional customers. Ripple says Virtu is among the firms trading the product. Clients can also cross-margin exposures with other supported assets and, where available, use its RLUSD stablecoin as collateral.

There is an important difference between these products and owning the underlying shares or barrels of oil. A perpetual swap provides derivative exposure, with funding, margin, counterparty and liquidation risks. Around-the-clock access does not mean the traditional market underneath is itself open for continuous price discovery.

For Ripple, this expands its position beyond payments and custody into cross-asset brokerage. For the wider tokenisation market, it points to a different path to 24/7 finance: institutions may first adopt crypto-native derivatives referencing familiar assets before the underlying securities infrastructure moves onchain. Availability is subject to jurisdiction and the offering’s stated licensing arrangements.

title: HSBC Warns Gold Has Failed as a Short-Term Volatility Hedge
summary: In a recent report, HSBC strategists stressed that while they expect gold prices to rise by year-end, the prime commodity has not been as effective as an equity hedge in 2026, largely because of the leveraged capital piled up behind gold investments. HSBC Critiques Gold Performance as an Equity Hedg...
content:
In a recent report, HSBC strategists stressed that while they expect gold prices to rise by year-end, the prime commodity has not been as effective as an equity hedge in 2026, largely because of the leveraged capital piled up behind gold investments.

Key Takeaways

  • HSBC warns gold is losing its short-term volatility hedge status as margin calls force investor sell-offs.
  • The bank remains bullish long-term, citing central bank buying and ETF inflows as key portfolio diversifiers.
  • Economists predict gold could reach $10,000 if the U.S. devalues its dollar to boost competitiveness.

HSBC Critiques Gold Performance as an Equity Hedge

While gold has enjoyed a multi-year bull run, with institutions predicting it could reach $6,300 per ounce in 2027, its role as a traditional hedge against market volatility has been debated this year.

HSBC, one of the world’s largest bullion-trading banks, recently issued a report explaining why gold has underperformed this year in an ecosystem that has seen risk assets like artificial intelligence and tech stocks swell.

“The ‘debasement trade’ of shifting capital into ‘hard assets’ such as gold can continue as concerns over debt and inflation linger,” HSBC analysts stressed, reinforcing the value of gold as a sound asset that can withstand large volatility levels even today.

The bank explained that as gold involvement in trading markets grows, its correlation with the wider stock markets also grows. “With leveraged capital crowded into gold, tumbling stocks trigger margin calls that force investors to unwind positions to raise cash,” analysts wrote.

“So although gold looks to be a robust hedge against systemic risks in a ‘multi-polar’ world, it’s not guaranteed to work as a short-term volatility dampener,” analysts warned, explaining that gold cannot become the common diversifier in each portfolio to weather each kind of market stress. Using other diversifiers remains a sound strategy for investors facing today’s uncertain market conditions, they said.

Gold prices have been holding at a resistance level, remaining near $4,000 per ounce. Even so, central banks have been consistently amassing gold in 2026, with this demand providing a cushion for prices to hold at relatively higher levels.

Taking this into consideration, HSBC concluded that “demand for portfolio diversification, central bank purchases, and steady ETF inflows continue to support our bullish view on gold and its role as a diversifier against broader portfolio risks.” Analysts added that they expect gold to end 2026 at a higher price level.

Economists like Jim Rickards have thrown out wild price predictions for gold, suggesting that it could touch $10,000 not only of increased demand but also a policy of devaluing the U.S. dollar—a strategy President Donald Trump has stressed makes America more competitive.

“You make a hell of a lot more money with a weaker dollar—not a weak dollar, but a weaker dollar—than you do with a strong dollar,” Trump said in July.

TL;DR: A BCG report commissioned by Ripple says custody buyers increasingly judge governance, interoperability and operational integration alongside asset security.

Institutional custody is becoming a question of how assets can be used, not just where keys are stored. Ripple’s October 21 discussion of a Boston Consulting Group research report argues that security is now a baseline requirement for banks and investment firms evaluating digital asset providers.

The report highlights policy controls, interoperability and the ability to connect custody with settlement, payments and treasury systems. BCG estimates that more than 30% of digital assets outside centralised exchanges are held through institutional custody models. That is an estimate from the commissioned research, rather than a directly observed count of every wallet in the market.

The shift matters for stablecoins and tokenised securities. Institutions may be comfortable with a technically secure wallet yet unable to deploy an asset if approval procedures, reporting or compatibility with existing systems are missing. Some firms could choose multiple custodians behind a shared orchestration layer; others may prefer integrated services.

Ripple sells custody infrastructure, so its framing is commercially interested and should be read as such. Nevertheless, the underlying question is pertinent across the industry. The winning custody model may be the one that makes conventional institutional controls possible without taking away the settlement advantages that attracted the bank to blockchain in the first place.

title: US OCC calls on community banks to become payment stablecoin issuers
summary: The announcement followed the banking regulator finalizing its rules for the GENIUS Act, a stablecoin law to be implemented in January
content:
The announcement followed the banking regulator finalizing its rules for the GENIUS Act, a stablecoin law to be implemented in January

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has petitioned community banks to enter the payment stablecoin market as part of the regulator’s rules on the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act.

In a Monday X post, the OCC said that it was “encouraging the development of payment stablecoin capabilities within the community banking sector,” citing its finalized rules for the GENIUS Act. The payment stablecoin law is set to be enforced starting in January, and the OCC finalized its rules for the bill last week.

“Interested community banks are encouraged to consider applying to become, or for a subsidiary to become, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, as applicable,” said the US banking regulator. 

The plea to community banks came as many banking advocacy groups pushed back against the OCC’s proposed rules on stablecoin yield, with some arguing that they went against the congressional intent behind GENIUS. If enough community banks were to enter the stablecoin market, they could challenge the market share of crypto companies and financial institutions.

Community banks are already engaged in legal action against the OCC over the regulator’s approval for charter applications from crypto companies. Earlier this month, the Independent Community Bankers of America filed a lawsuit alleging that crypto companies had an advantage over community bankers by not being subject to the same regulatory requirements.

title: Injective launches onchain futures market tracking Nvidia GPU rental costs
summary: The new index tracks rental prices for five Nvidia GPUs, offering leveraged trading and potential hedging against fluctuations in AI computing costs.
content:
Layer-1 blockchain Injective has launched a perpetual futures market tracking the rental prices of five Nvidia GPUs, allowing traders to bet on changes in AI computing costs with up to 10x leverage.

The Super Intelligence Compute Index (SICI) tracks rental prices for Nvidia’s H100, B200, H200, A100 and RTX 4090 chips, using data from compute marketplaces compiled by London-based market data firm LO:TECH.

According to Monday’s announcement, the index assigns the largest weight to the H100 at 40%, followed by the B200 at 25%. It is updated hourly using a trailing seven-day average of rental prices. Traders can take positions on whether the index will rise or fall, using USDC as margin.

The launch builds on Injective’s August 2025 introduction of a market tied to Nvidia H100 rental prices, expanding the offering from a single GPU model to a five-chip index.

Companies developing AI models often rent computing power from cloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius rather than purchasing Nvidia GPUs outright. As rental prices rise and fall with demand, Injective said the futures market could help developers hedge against higher computing costs while allowing GPU providers to protect against declining rental revenue.

Related: Injective, BDACS plan Korean won stablecoin settlement for tokenized assets 

AI infrastructure boom raises financial concerns

The launch comes as companies renting out AI computing power face questions about whether they can recover the cost of building and operating GPU infrastructure.

Research firm Gartner warned in October that more than 80% of specialist AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, could cease operating independently by 2030 as they struggle to generate sufficient returns on their investments.

Elon Musk echoed those concerns Sunday, saying more than 200 neocloud providers could face failure or consolidation as lenders become reluctant to finance companies dependent on AI data center revenue.

Musk has financial interests in the sector through SpaceX, whose “Super Intelligence” business recently reported $7.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 830% year over year, partly driven by new cloud services agreements.

Source: Elon Musk

Meanwhile, major technology companies are restructuring their operations to contain costs as they pour billions of dollars into AI infrastructure.

On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft, which has forecast roughly $175 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 eligible employees as it seeks to reduce costs amid rising AI infrastructure spending.

Meta, which has already invested more than $100 billion in AI, cut 8,000 jobs in May as part of a restructuring aimed at reducing costs.

title: Blink Wallet Adds Inactivity Fee to Custodial Accounts, Accelerating Migration to Self Custody
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

Blink Wallet Adds Inactivity Fee to Custodial Accounts, Accelerating Migration to Self Custody
Blink Wallet began charging a $1 monthly fee on custodial accounts inactive for 12 months, with the first charges processed by mid-October 2026 and full refunds on login.
This post Blink ...
content:
Blink Wallet announced a new $1 a month inactivity fee, aimed at custodial accounts that have not logged in to the app in over 12 months. 

The decision was put into motion in early September via a Terms of Service change, with push notifications sent out to inactive users, and the first charge made by mid-October. Fees charged will be refunded if users log back in within 12 months, according to a blog post published by the company. 

The fee, which only affects custodial accounts, serves to relieve the burden of inactive accounts on the startup. According to the announcement, these inactive accounts have ongoing costs such as “ledger and infrastructure, retention of verification records, compliance monitoring and reporting, and support claims.” These costs are in turn borne by active user accounts via normal in-app transaction fees. 

A source familiar with the matter told Bitcoin Magazine that around a hundred thousand such accounts fit the inactive category at the time of the first fee charge, with an aggregate balance of over $800,000. The first fee pulled in about $45,000, mostly from accounts that had dust amounts of bitcoin inactive for over a year. None of these figures could be independently verified. 

A Bit of History

Blink Wallet may be one of the most popular Bitcoin wallets in the world, favored by advocates of Bitcoin Circular Economies across Latin America and Africa. Designed for an audience not already familiar with Bitcoin, the wallet first came to prominence as the ‘Bitcoin Beach Wallet’. It grew out of El Salvador’s initial wave of Bitcoin adoption, choosing design principles similar to Wallet of Satoshi, which had seen viral success in earlier years. The wallet was initially custodial and oriented around fast Lightning payments, with the innovative option of hedging value in USD via the Stable Sats feature.

Historically, custodial wallets have seen accelerated early growth compared to their non-custodial counterparts. It is arguably due to the friction introduced by non-custodial setup steps like the 12-word backup, but also by the lack of key material under the company’s control, which enabled features like the first generation of Stable Sats in the first place.

Because of the smooth interface and user experience Blink offered, it quickly became a favorite for evangelists to recommend. One particular evangelist allegedly got everyone he met to download the app and gave them about $1 worth of bitcoin. Some of those new users might have stuck around. But events like today’s Blink announcement put into question the effectiveness of such evangelism strategies, given that they may just be turned into dormant dust accounts. 

Blink was eventually spun off from Galoy Inc its founding firm, to be run by Lukas Duczko and a new board of directors. The announcement published in October 2024 stated that Duczko now had a controlling stake in the company, while Galoy continued to be a service provider and minority stakeholder. The Bitcoin Beach Fund was also established at the time, seeded with Blink shares as part of the transaction. The wallet once headquartered in El Salvador is now based in the free economic zone of Roatán, Honduras, though it maintains corporate entities in El Salvador and the United States.

Headwinds

Despite its success gaining international adoption among Bitcoin circular economies, evangelists and supporters of the Lightning Network, the company has also faced significant headwinds. And not just Blink but custodial wallets in general, like Wallet of Satoshi, Alby, and Blue Wallet, all phased out their custodial wallet offerings in recent years, pivoting to self custody infrastructure like Spark. The tide began to rise with the EU’s MiCA regulations, which sought licensing and KYC compliance standards from custodians that these wallets simply could not provide. 

On the U.S. side of the pond, the Samourai Wallet case and the broader war on crypto by the Biden administration pushed wallet operators outside of the country, with notable examples like Phoenix Wallet, Wallet of Satoshi, Wasabi Wallet, and Blink, limiting or altogether exiting American app stores. The legal uncertainty took place under the shadow of the Samourai Wallet and Tornado Cash cases, which the industry read as threats to user privacy and certainly to self custody wallets, let alone custodial ones. 

Fast forward a couple of years and Google Play decided to enforce EU and American laws by limiting Play Store distribution of wallets or exchange apps that do not hold licenses in corresponding jurisdictions. The viral nature and stunningly easy-to-use apps that were possible thanks to custodial Lightning had, in a matter of 2 years, become a liability. It was time to pivot to self custody. 

Nobody Said it was Easy

By 2025, Blink’s counterparts already offered self custody options; WOS was beginning to push their Spark-powered wallet, with 2027 as the deadline for custody wallet users to migrate. Alby had shipped a feature to connect self-hosted Lightning nodes to its hub and shut down its custodial Lightning option. Blue wallet had long ago shut down its custodial offer and had since doubled down on becoming an onchain wallet for new and power users alike.

Unlike its competitors, however, Blink’s biggest differentiator is the Stable Sats feature, which likely required a significant redesign to fit the limitations of self custody. It wasn’t until June 2026 that Blink launched its Spark supported self custodial wallet, a big move and one that its user base is still adapting to. 

To make things worse, on September 19th, hackers managed to withdraw 6.61 bitcoins from custodial wallet users via compromised admin tools. The company’s backers quickly announced they would make the affected users whole, and the bleeding was stopped, but the blow nevertheless must have shaken the company. 

Remarkably, despite some of the most difficult years for the Bitcoin wallet industry, Blink wallet has so far not just survived but stayed in the game. It has retained the slick design that made it so popular, while delivering advanced features that users in developing nations need, such as dollar-denominated value at the speed of lightning, meanwhile pivoting to self custody. The inactivity fee is but an inevitable step further down that transition. Perhaps having teams like Blink’s working on self custody will yield a new crop of sovereign technologies, its fruits badly needed by a sector of the industry battered by regulators and now AI cyber threats.

TL;DR: Solana’s October 16 changelog confirms Web3.js v3.1 alongside validator-client releases and developer tooling updates.

A major blockchain upgrade attracts the headlines, but everyday development friction can hold back adoption just as effectively. Solana’s October 16 changelog confirms the arrival of Web3.js v3.1, an update intended to work more closely with the growing set of tools used to build applications on the network.

The release improves interoperability with Solana Kit, Wallet Adapter, Surfpool, Anchor, Codama and SPL interfaces. For application teams, the attraction is not a promised jump in token prices; it is having fewer incompatible pieces between wallet interaction, transaction construction and local testing.

The same changelog lists Agave and Firedancer releases, updates to testing libraries and discussion of validator performance. It also describes proposals around computation limits and post-Alpenglow improvements. Those proposals should not be mistaken for features that have already been deployed. In particular, release numbers and discussion notes describe several distinct stages of the protocol’s engineering pipeline.

Developer experience rarely translates into an immediate market catalyst. It can, however, change the cost of shipping a working financial product. As Solana asks builders to support more complicated payments and tokenised assets, a stable, interoperable JavaScript library is part of the infrastructure that makes those use cases realistic.

title: Solana’s Next Latency Idea Has a Geographic Trade-Off Validators Cannot Ignore
summary: Research into a geo-aware leader schedule suggests quicker validator handovers, but also warns that grouping leaders by location introduces security trade-

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Research into a geo-aware leader schedule suggests quicker validator handovers, but also warns that grouping leaders by location introduces security trade-offs.

Solana’s push for lower latency is moving beyond shorter slots. A new study of SIMD-0675 considers rearranging its validator leader schedule so that consecutive leaders are more likely to be geographically close, reducing the time it takes information to travel between them.

This is not a proposal to give particular validators more production slots. The researchers keep each validator’s allocation unchanged and instead reconsider the order in which those windows occur. Their analysis uses 6,250 synthetic networks based on the chain’s existing 124 validator locations.

The appealing result is a reduction in average handover delay, around 29 milliseconds in one highlighted configuration. But grouping leaders by proximity can leave the schedule concentrated in one region for longer. Because validator locations are declared, it also creates an incentive to misreport geography. The study weighs these costs against the milliseconds saved and identifies a relatively modest grouping range as a potential compromise.

The work remains research, not evidence that this scheduling system has been activated on mainnet. It shows how scaling decisions get harder as a network becomes faster: shaving milliseconds is useful, but only if the randomness and geographical distribution that help preserve resilience are not quietly sacrificed.

title: Canada opens consultation on stablecoins, citing US GENIUS Act
summary: As part of the potential implementation of its Stablecoin Act, the Canadian government will hear from the public on a proposed framework for tokens from non-financial institutions.
content:
Lawmakers in the Canadian government opened a 60-day public consultation on regulations proposed to address non-financial institution stablecoin issuers, including a potential prohibition on yield payments.

On Saturday, the government of Canada gave notice that it would be open to public comment on the stablecoin regulations until Dec. 23. The proposed framework cited efforts to be consistent with stablecoin regulations in the United States and other jurisdictions, to “reduce the overall regulatory burden on multi-jurisdictional issuers.”

Notably, the proposed regulations said that non-financial institution stablecoin issuers would be restricted from offering interest or yield to discourage HODLing the tokens. They would also be required to redeem stablecoins within three business days of requests from tokenholders, and not charge a fee greater than 1% of the coins’ total value.

The regulations fell under Canada’s Stablecoin Act, which was passed in March and intended to address non-financial institution issuers. According to the government, the proposed rules were required to enact the policy and include provisions for issuers to register with Canada’s central bank.

“The intention is for the proposed Regulations to come into force in fall 2027,” said the government. “Once the proposed Regulations are in effect, issuers of stablecoins in Canada who are not financial institutions would be required to apply for registration with the Bank of Canada prior to issuing a stablecoin.”

The GENIUS Act, which establishes a regulatory framework for stablecoins in the US, is scheduled to take effect in January 2027. Meanwhile, the European Union’s regulations, Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA), could give exchanges until January to halt services for stablecoins not in compliance with the framework, likely including Tether’s USDt (USDT), the largest stablecoin by market capitalization.

Related: Bank of Canada lays out criteria for ‘good money’ stablecoins

title: Tokenised US Stock Venues Must Give 30 Days’ Public Notice, SEC Clarifies
summary: SEC staff guidance spells out a 30-day public-notice requirement for venues seeking to operate under the temporary tokenised-stock exemption.

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: SEC staff guidance spells out a 30-day public-notice requirement for venues seeking to operate under the temporary tokenised-stock exemption.

The SEC’s experiment with blockchain-based stock trading comes with a meaningful preparation period. Guidance published on October 20 says a tokenised securities venue relying on the agency’s conditional innovation exemption must publish a public operating notice at least 30 calendar days before starting.

The document does more than specify a deadline. It says venues should have their operations and access standards ready for production when they disclose them, and must keep the notice accurate as details change. A platform cannot simply announce that it intends to trade tokenised shares and treat that as permission to begin immediately.

There are issuer protections too. Where a venue proposes to trade shares tokenised by a third party, a separate objection period may still be running. The SEC staff says the venue can disclose that pending status, but cannot make those shares available before the relevant period concludes without an objection.

Importantly, these are staff FAQs interpreting a conditional order, not a generally applicable new rule with the force of law. The exemption remains limited in scope. Its wider significance is that US regulators are testing whether distributed-ledger market infrastructure can be introduced with ordinary disclosure, investor rights and accountability still visible to the public.

title: AI company Anthropic announces IPO, expected as early as November
summary: The artificial intelligence company disclosed more than $16 billion in revenue and an $80 billion net loss for the first half of 2026.
content:
The artificial intelligence company disclosed more than $16 billion in revenue and an $80 billion net loss for the first half of 2026.

Anthropic announced that it had filed S-1 registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for an initial public offering on Nasdaq, marking a significant step for artificial intelligence companies.

A Monday S-1 filing with the SEC suggested that Anthropic could be aiming for a mid-November IPO, listing its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. The company disclosed more than $16 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026 and an $80 billion net loss over the same period.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by many former executives of AI company OpenAI. Reports have suggested that the company could raise up to $100 billion for an IPO, giving it a $2 trillion valuation. OpenAI has already delayed its own IPO plans, with CEO Sam Altman reportedly saying in September that 2026 was an “ill-advised moment” to pursue a public offering.

The company behind the AI assistant Claude reported holding more than $112 billion in cash and cash equivalents, along with $19 billion in short-term investments, as of June 30.

title: NBA names Kalshi, Polymarket preferred exchanges, signs CFTC deal
summary: The US professional basketball league is expanding into prediction markets with official data agreements and safeguards against insider trading.
content:
The National Basketball Association has named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred prediction market exchanges and signed an information-sharing agreement with the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) aimed at protecting the integrity of basketball-related markets.

According to Monday’s announcement, the agreements will give Kalshi and Polymarket access to official NBA data supplied by Sportradar, the league’s designated data distribution partner, for settling authorized markets. Both platforms will have rights to use NBA intellectual property and conduct promotional activities in the United States.

The partnerships include integrity safeguards, prohibiting NBA and team personnel from trading NBA event contracts and requiring cooperation on suspicious trading investigations.

Beyond the two exchanges, the NBA expanded its existing agreement with DraftKings to cover prediction markets and said it expects to announce similar arrangements with other industry operators in the coming weeks.

In a separate announcement, CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said the agreement with the NBA would strengthen information sharing to address insider trading and fraud in prediction markets. The NBA joins Major League Baseball and the National Hockey League in establishing similar arrangements with the regulator.

Related: Kalshi strikes deal with S&P Dow Jones Indices to expand financial event contracts

States challenge federal oversight of prediction markets

The NBA’s agreements come amid an ongoing legal battle over whether federal commodities rules supersede state gambling laws governing sports prediction markets.

The dispute has produced conflicting court decisions. In September, the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against Kalshi in a case involving Ohio and Tennessee, following a similar decision by the 9th Circuit. An earlier ruling by the 3rd Circuit, however, allowed Kalshi to continue operating in New Jersey while its appeal proceeds.

State enforcement actions have continued. On Oct. 20, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown sued Kalshi, alleging that the platform had facilitated illegal betting in the state since 2024. Utah officials are seeking to recover an estimated $30 million to $60 million in profits allegedly earned by Kalshi and other defendants.

Kalshi event contract. Source: Kalshi

The US Supreme Court has been asked to review the New Jersey dispute, with 39 states and Washington, DC, supporting the petition. The National Football League, which has not entered into commercial partnerships with prediction market exchanges, also backed the petition, arguing that certain sports event contracts threaten game integrity because they are susceptible to manipulation. The justices have not yet agreed to hear the case.
